subjects.label: Legislative Assembly, political trajectory and loss of authority
subjects.meaning: The Assembly began with locally experienced but nationally little-known deputies, drove confrontation over priests, émigrés, and war, and then lost practical authority to popular and communal power before the Convention met. Its deputies were often nationally obscure but had acquired revolutionary administrative experience; composition belongs within this institutional trajectory.
subjects.stance: The source rejects the departing deputies' condescension toward the new body, but shows that its authority collapsed during the crises it helped create.
acceptable_access: Legislative Assembly, political trajectory and loss of authority

evidence.evidence_summary: Introduces the Assembly's social composition, local revolutionary experience, and priorities.
Provides the Assembly's occupational, social, generational, and experiential profile.
Clerical resistance and emigration are identified as the deputies' most urgent opening problems.
Deposition and Lafayette questions move beyond the deputies' ability to manage them.
The Assembly watches the 10 August insurrection helplessly and suspends the monarchy after the palace falls.
With most deputies absent, the remaining Assembly yields to the new Paris Commune during its final weeks.

subjects.label: Louis XVI and the breakdown of constitutional monarchy
subjects.meaning: Royal vetoes, conflicting war calculations, and repeated confrontations with ministers, deputies, and popular demonstrators destroyed trust in the constitutional settlement and culminated in suspension of the monarchy.
subjects.stance: The king sometimes acted from defensible constitutional motives and showed personal courage, but his conduct and secret hopes made durable constitutional reconciliation impossible.
acceptable_access: Louis XVI and the breakdown of constitutional monarchy

evidence.evidence_summary: The king's veto of the émigré decree ends the early accommodation with the Assembly.
His veto of the nonjuror decree deepens suspicion even as he supports pressure leading toward war.
Louis dismisses Roland, Servan and Clavière on 13 June; Dumouriez follows on 15 June before taking a field command.
Louis withstands the armed demonstration of 20 June but cannot restore lasting confidence in the constitution.
The 10 August assault destroys royal authority and brings formal suspension of the monarchy.

subjects.label: Road to war and declaration of war, October 1791–April 1792
subjects.meaning: Pressure against émigré bases, Brissotin claims that war would consolidate the Revolution, royal counter-revolutionary hopes, and Austrian-Prussian diplomacy produced the declaration of war on 20 April 1792.
subjects.stance: War emerged from incompatible expectations and escalating choices rather than a single coherent national purpose; its public defensive pledges were soon broken.
acceptable_access: Road to war and declaration of war, October 1791–April 1792

evidence.evidence_summary: Brissot links suppression of émigré support abroad to the possibility of war.
The king, Lafayette, Narbonne, and Brissotins discover different advantages in confrontation.
The Trier ultimatum wins broad political support while Brissot and Robespierre define opposing cases for war.
Clootz proclaims the imminent liberation of Europe and encourages war fever among foreign exiles.
Austrian threats and the Prussian alliance intensify demands for direct war against the Habsburg ruler.
A pro-war ministry removes the final political obstacles, and only seven deputies oppose the declaration.
His notoriety and international identity contribute to his election to the Convention.

subjects.label: Paris sections, sansculottes, and popular sovereignty
subjects.meaning: Economic strain and war revived inclusive sectional politics, enabled coordination with fédérés, democratized the National Guard, and shifted effective sovereignty from elected deputies toward armed popular institutions. The Cordeliers were a specific coordinating center within this wider movement; opening sections and the National Guard broadened participation, while claims to represent the sovereign people could conflict with representative institutions.
subjects.stance: The source treats organized popular power as decisive in overthrowing the monarchy while also emphasizing intimidation, vengeance, and coercion.
acceptable_access: Paris sections, sansculottes, and popular sovereignty
artisans and tradesmen in the Revolution

evidence.evidence_summary: Service in the Guard provided new deputies with practical revolutionary experience.
The royal guard, regular troops, Paris officers, and proposed provincial camp become competing security projects.
Popular societies multiply, sectional petitioning revives, and new radical leaders emerge during the spring crisis.
Eastern sections coordinate their mass demonstration from the Cordeliers.
Sections admit citizens without property distinctions, sit continuously, and coordinate with the fédérés.
Arming all citizens and opening the National Guard give the popular movement the means to demand deposition.
The insurrectionary Commune compels the legislature to suspend monarchy and convoke a Convention.
After 10 August the Commune and sansculotte demands dominate the remnant of the Legislative Assembly.
Prison-plot fears and popular justice lead sans-culottes into the first massacre attacks.
Artisans carry out killings they believe necessary, then volunteer for the front in large numbers.
The Convention is framed as a new assembly formed to secure popular sovereignty, but through a mediated electoral process.
Debate over trying the king turns on whether popular judgment was already complete or required representative procedure.
Fear of renewed sans-culotte action forms part of the environment surrounding the king's sentence.

subjects.label: Demonstration of 20 June 1792
subjects.meaning: An armed sectional demonstration invaded the Tuileries to demand ministerial reinstatement and pressure the king, failed in its immediate aims, but rehearsed the method and sharpened the alignments of the decisive August confrontation.
subjects.stance: Immediate failure became a turning point because it exposed the constitution's exhaustion and taught the organizers how a later insurrection would need to proceed.

evidence.evidence_summary: Between ten and twenty thousand armed demonstrators enter the palace, confront the king, and leave without securing their demands.
The event and its lessons are presented as establishing the form of the next, decisive confrontation.
The tocsin and remembered popular days of 1789 provide the signal and model for insurrection.

relationships.rationale: Immediate failure provides a rehearsal and organizational lessons.

subjects.label: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and fall of the monarchy
subjects.meaning: The sectional central committee became an insurrectionary Commune, sent fédérés and the democratized National Guard against the Tuileries, defeated the Swiss Guards, and forced suspension of the monarchy.
subjects.stance: The source presents 10 August as the bloodiest and most decisive revolutionary journée to that point, transferring power away from king and Assembly alike.
acceptable_access: Insurrection of 10 August 1792 and fall of the monarchy

evidence.evidence_summary: The Brunswick threats, distribution of arms, deposition petitions, and Brissotin retreat prepare the insurrection.
The Commune's forces take the Tuileries, destroy the Swiss garrison, and cause the Assembly to suspend the monarchy.
Effective power after the uprising lies with the Paris Commune rather than the Assembly.
Surviving defenders later form one politically identified group among massacre victims.

relationships.rationale: The overthrow suspends monarchy and confines the royal family.

subjects.label: September Massacres
subjects.meaning: Fear of invasion and a prison conspiracy, radical advocacy, and communal coordination produced improvised prison tribunals and the killing of roughly half the Paris prison population from 2 to 7 September, followed by killings at Versailles.
subjects.stance: The killers and Commune regarded the violence as necessary, but most victims were not politically dangerous and the massacres horrified observers and poisoned factional politics.

evidence.evidence_summary: Front-line panic and fear of prison breakouts trigger attacks, improvised tribunals, and mass killing in the Paris prisons.
The source identifies the varied victims, limited political danger of most, communal approval, European horror, and enduring factional blame.

relationships.rationale: Mutual blame becomes a durable factional weapon.

subjects.label: Battle of Valmy
subjects.meaning: Volunteer mobilization, superior French artillery, and determined national enthusiasm stopped the Prussian advance on 20 September 1792 and transformed the political and military crisis.
subjects.stance: Valmy is presented as proof that revolutionary motivation could alter established warfare, though the French also held concrete numerical and artillery advantages.

evidence.evidence_summary: The French outnumber and outgun the Prussians and fight with exceptional enthusiasm to halt the invasion.
Goethe, present with the Duke of Weimar, frames the French stand as the birth of a new epoch.
The Prussians open negotiations immediately, and the event is framed as the beginning of a new historical epoch.

relationships.rationale: Valmy and the Convention’s opening coincide; monarchy is abolished the following day.

subjects.label: National Convention and establishment of the Republic
subjects.meaning: The Convention was elected through two-stage voting under broad but restricted male suffrage, with low turnout and substantial continuity in experienced political personnel. It met on 20 September 1792, abolished monarchy on 21 September, and the subsequent republican calendar began Year I on 22 September.
subjects.stance: Wider franchise did not eliminate social selectivity or political continuity. Use the precise dates on page 194 to distinguish meeting, abolition and the later calendar epoch.
acceptable_access: National Convention and establishment of the Republic

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly orders Convention elections by broad male suffrage; turnout is low and many experienced deputies return.
Sets out the suffrage rules, two-stage election, emergency timing, turnout, and returning deputies.
The Convention abolishes monarchy on 21 September and anchors Year I of the Republic in September 1792.
Describes the Convention's age, occupations, property base, limited artisan representation, and accumulated political experience.

subjects.label: Trial and execution of Louis XVI
subjects.meaning: The Convention rejected claims of royal inviolability, tried Louis before the representatives of the sovereign people, found him guilty, rejected an appeal to the people and reprieve, and executed him on 21 January 1793.
subjects.stance: Guilt was virtually uncontested, while punishment and popular ratification divided the Convention; intimidation may have affected close votes but did not erase political agency.
acceptable_access: Trial and execution of Louis XVI
Louis XVI, sentence and popular appeal

evidence.evidence_summary: Evidence against the king, legal problems of inviolability, and Montagnard arguments lead toward a Convention trial.
The indictment, defense, guilty verdict, and defeat of the Girondin appeal to the people define the trial's political stakes.
Close roll calls settle death and reject reprieve before the king's execution on 21 January.

relationships.rationale: Execution makes the revolutionary rupture harder to reverse.

subjects.label: Regicide and the irreversible Republican Revolution
subjects.meaning: The execution of Louis XVI completed the chapter's republican transformation by foreclosing compromise and strengthening both domestic and European enemies of the Revolution.
subjects.stance: Regicide is interpreted less as a settled victory than as an irrevocable challenge that intensified the conflicts of 1793.
acceptable_access: Regicide and the irreversible Republican Revolution

evidence.evidence_summary: The chapter opens with a new legislature shaped by post-1789 local experience and hostility toward perceived domestic enemies.
Peasants act to make feudal destruction irreversible, and the newly begun war is said to do still more toward that end.
The failed June confrontation and preparations for another make the constitutional settlement appear exhausted.
The 10 August victory suspends monarchy and transfers effective power away from the legislature.
Valmy coincides with the Convention's meeting and immediate declaration of a republic.
The chapter concludes that execution made the destruction of the old regime irrevocable while multiplying the Republic's enemies.

subjects.label: Refractory priests and anti-clerical legislation
subjects.meaning: Non-juring clergy were treated as a central domestic threat; successive measures moved from surveillance and loss of pensions toward exile, deportation, arrest, and exclusion from religious facilities.
subjects.stance: Provincial conflict and war panic radicalized policy, while royal vetoes intensified suspicions that the king protected counter-revolution.

evidence.evidence_summary: Local revolutionary authorities identify refractory priests as a major domestic problem before the Assembly convenes.
Large-scale oath refusal in the Vendee confirms the issue's urgency.
The Assembly orders a new oath, surveillance, and possible exile; Louis XVI vetoes the decree.
Military reverses prompt a renewed decree allowing deportation of denounced nonjurors.
After 10 August the Assembly orders nonjurors to leave France and makes even some non-oath-bound clergy vulnerable to deportation.
More than two hundred priests are among the massacre victims.

subjects.label: Émigrés and counter-revolutionary pressure
subjects.meaning: Growing emigration, armed émigré groups across the frontier, confiscatory legislation, and foreign protection made émigrés a catalyst of confrontation between Assembly, king, and European rulers.
subjects.stance: The émigrés were politically potent as symbols and pretexts even when their direct military capacity was weak.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly confronts accelerating emigration and armed counter-revolutionary organization beyond the frontier.
The 9 November decree sequesters revenues and threatens absent citizens with capital penalties, but the king vetoes it.
The Assembly redirects pressure toward German rulers harboring armed emigres.
The Trier ultimatum briefly removes the immediate émigré pretext for war.
The émigré princes are charged with treason as war agitation shifts toward Austria.

subjects.label: Feuillants and Jacobins, changing political influence
subjects.meaning: The initially larger Feuillant affiliation declined because private, cautious politics offered little public influence, while the Jacobins became the arena where prominent figures and new deputies shaped national debate.
subjects.stance: Public political practice and reputation, not initial membership totals, explain the Jacobins' ascendancy and Feuillant collapse.
acceptable_access: Feuillants and Jacobins, changing political influence

evidence.evidence_summary: The Feuillants begin with more affiliated deputies but exclude spectators and lack visible leadership.
Feuillant membership melts away while nationally important debate and political apprenticeship concentrate at the Jacobins.
Nightly debate pits Brissot's war program against Robespierre's objections.
Feuillant leaders and Robespierre oppose the increasingly dominant pro-war course from different positions.
Replacement ministers are dismissed as weak Feuillant figures associated with Lafayette.
The club increasingly supports overthrow by insurrection, with Robespierre joining the call for direct action.
The massacres become material for factional accusation within Jacobin politics.

subjects.label: Brissot, the Brissotins, and revolutionary war
subjects.meaning: Brissot and allied Bordeaux deputies made war the proposed solution to émigré threats, domestic division, and revolutionary legitimacy, formed the pro-war ministry, and later became identified as the Gironde.
subjects.stance: Their optimistic war rhetoric helped produce a conflict for which France was unprepared, and their tactical use of popular pressure later exposed them to radical suspicion.
acceptable_access: Brissot, the Brissotins, and revolutionary war

evidence.evidence_summary: Brissot proposes attacking the foreign protectors of émigrés if confiscatory pressure fails.
Brissot and the Bordeaux group portray war as national regeneration and a test of royal loyalty.
The March ministry consists largely of Brissot's pro-war nominees and clears the way for war.
The Gironde recoils from total overthrow after earlier hoping popular pressure would restore its ministers.
Conflict with the Commune and Robespierre fixes the label 'faction of the Gironde.'

subjects.label: Robespierre, opposition to war and turn to insurrection
subjects.meaning: Robespierre warned that war could empower generals or the court, then abandoned constitutional defense as invasion and popular mobilization made insurrection appear necessary, before leading attacks on the Gironde.
subjects.stance: His anti-war warnings were isolated but prescient; his later radical turn was contingent on the July crisis rather than continuous from the spring.
acceptable_access: Robespierre, opposition to war and turn to insurrection
Robespierre and trial of Louis XVI

evidence.evidence_summary: Robespierre warns that victory could produce military dictatorship and defeat could enable royal counter-revolution.
He continues opposing escalation even after Austrian threats strengthen the war party.
On 29 July he endorses direct action against the monarchy after months of constitutional defense.
He attacks Brissot's circle as the Girondin faction during the Commune-Assembly struggle.
He adopts the claim that the people already judged Louis on 10 August and that only punishment remains.
He argues that a conventional trial risks placing the Revolution itself under judgment.

relationships.rationale: Robespierre disputes Brissot’s regenerative war case.

subjects.label: Royal court, Austrian Committee suspicions, and secret war aims
subjects.meaning: Secret royal correspondence and the court's hope that military defeat would reverse the Revolution sustained belief in an Austrian Committee and made military setbacks appear evidence of treason.
subjects.stance: Distinguish the particular Austrian Committee rumor from actual secret correspondence: the queen sought confrontation for political recovery rather than simply Austrian protection for the émigrés. Evidence of correspondence does not validate every palace conspiracy accusation.
acceptable_access: Royal court, Austrian Committee suspicions, and secret war aims

evidence.evidence_summary: The royal veto is interpreted by Brissot's circle as proof of a secret Austrian-led conspiracy.
The queen seeks confrontation, while king and generals expect war to enable revolutionary defeat and domestic restoration.
The queen's indifference to constitutional pacification contributes to Barnave's withdrawal and continued mistrust.
Public revolutionary aims are contrasted with the royal family's and generals' secret expectations.
Early defeats revive claims that king, generals, and the Austrian Committee are betraying France.

subjects.label: Austria and Prussia, diplomacy and invasion of France
subjects.meaning: Austrian threats, the Austro-Prussian alliance, delayed coalition preparations, the Brunswick declaration, and advances through Longwy and Verdun framed the domestic revolution of 1792.
subjects.stance: The coalition's intimidating diplomacy and invasion radicalized France, while its slow, divided military strategy created space for revolutionary recovery.
acceptable_access: Austria and Prussia, diplomacy and invasion of France
Leopold II and French war crisis

evidence.evidence_summary: Austrian threats and the defensive pact with Prussia harden the French drive to war.
A defiant Austrian reply, ministerial collapse, and Austrian mobilization remove remaining obstacles to war.
Austrian caution and delayed Prussian entry postpone a coordinated advance despite French battlefield failures.
The Brunswick declaration threatens Paris and openly links coalition war aims to restoration of royal authority.
The fall of Longwy intensifies invasion panic and mass arrest in Paris.
After Valmy the Prussians negotiate and withdraw when the new Convention declares a republic.

relationships.rationale: Austrian threats and alliance calculations accelerate escalation.

subjects.label: Saint-Domingue slave uprising and colonial crisis
subjects.meaning: The August 1791 slave revolt grew into a complex civil war, exposed incoherent French policy on slavery and free people of color, and produced immediate political and commodity-price consequences in France.
subjects.stance: The source identifies it as the world's greatest and only successful slave rebellion and connects colonial crisis directly to metropolitan politics and markets.
acceptable_access: Saint-Domingue slave uprising and colonial crisis
rights of free people of color

evidence.evidence_summary: Describes the uprising's scale, roots in racial and constitutional conflict, delayed communications, and effect on Brissot and Bordeaux.

relationships.rationale: Colonial disruption causes sugar scarcity and popular price fixing.

subjects.label: Food shortages, inflation, assignats, and popular price action
subjects.meaning: Colonial sugar scarcity, grain redistribution, falling currency values, and rising prices produced female-led price fixing, grain riots, attacks on warehouses, and demands for controls on hoarders.
subjects.stance: Keep distinct mechanisms visible: Saint-Domingue disruption drove sugar scarcity and female price-fixing, capital stockpiling depleted surrounding grain supplies, and currency depreciation raised prices. This local economic-action requirement should not disappear inside a whole-book assignat lifecycle.
acceptable_access: Food shortages, inflation, assignats, and popular price action

evidence.evidence_summary: The Saint-Domingue crisis triples sugar prices and prompts largely female crowds to impose old prices in Paris.
Grain disorders, the Étampes lynching, Dunkirk destruction, and depreciation of the livre and assignats show widening economic crisis.
Spring shortages revive popular societies and give Jacques Roux an audience for controls and attacks on hoarders.

relationships.rationale: Provisioning and prices renew popular political organization.

subjects.label: Southern rural violence and defense of anti-feudal gains
subjects.meaning: Conflict around Marseilles, Arles, Avignon, and Pont Saint-Esprit triggered attacks on non-juring priests, nobles, castles, and feudal records across the Midi in spring 1792.
subjects.stance: The precise meaning is uncertain, but the source cautiously interprets the attacks as peasant action to make the destruction of the old social order irreversible when central authority failed.
acceptable_access: Southern rural violence and defense of anti-feudal gains

evidence.evidence_summary: The Arles conflict and Pont Saint-Esprit drownings trigger widespread attacks on suspected counter-revolutionaries and property.
Destruction of castles and feudal records spreads across the south and is cautiously linked to fear that the gains of 1789 could be reversed.

subjects.label: Early French military defeats and treason panic
subjects.meaning: The failed April offensive, troop indiscipline, desertion, and murder of a general produced Parisian scapegoating, conspiracy claims, and emergency measures against foreigners, priests, and the royal guard.
subjects.stance: Political rhetoric had concealed military weakness; reverses were recast as treason rather than faced as failures of preparation.
acceptable_access: Early French military defeats and treason panic

evidence.evidence_summary: The first Belgian advance collapses, and French troops kill a commander they suspect of betrayal.
French units break at first resistance, kill a suspected commander, and prompt denunciations and restrictive decrees in Paris.
Enemy invasion and the Brunswick threat intensify democratization and the deposition movement.
The fall of Longwy leads to searches, arrests, and prison overcrowding.
Verdun's danger triggers panic and the opening attacks on prisoners.
After the internal purge, popular volunteering and Valmy connect domestic mobilization to military recovery.

subjects.label: Girondin ministry and ministerial crisis of March–June 1792
subjects.meaning: The March ministry favored war and brought Roland, Servan, Clavière and Dumouriez to prominence. Louis dismissed Roland, Servan and Clavière on 13 June; Dumouriez followed on 15 June and took an army command. Replacement ministers were associated with the Feuillants and Lafayette.
subjects.stance: The ministerial rupture intensified popular and royal conflict. Do not infer that the king dismissed Dumouriez together with the other three ministers.
acceptable_access: Girondin ministry and ministerial crisis of March–June 1792

evidence.evidence_summary: Ministerial replacement places war advocates in office before the declaration.
Three ministers are dismissed on 13 June; Dumouriez follows on 15 June and obtains field command.

relationships.rationale: Ministerial dismissals help provoke the June demonstration.

subjects.label: Lafayette, military intervention and political collapse
subjects.meaning: Lafayette favored war as a route to military and domestic restoration, was repeatedly suspected of dictatorship, intervened against Jacobins, failed to rally support, and defected after 10 August.
subjects.stance: His actions made fears of military dictatorship politically credible, yet his attempted intervention failed with both Assembly and royal family.
acceptable_access: Lafayette, military intervention and political collapse

evidence.evidence_summary: Lafayette expects war to restore the army and enable domestic stability.
Robespierre identifies a successful Lafayette as a potential military dictator.
Security measures and military reorganization are shaped by fear of a coup associated with him.
His letter attacking the Jacobins reinforces suspicion that he plans a military coup.
He comes to Paris after 20 June but fails to rally the National Guard or win royal support.
After 10 August he abandons a possible march on Paris and surrenders to the Prussians.

subjects.label: Fédérés and national revolutionary mobilization
subjects.meaning: Provincial National Guard volunteers converged on Paris, joined sectional politics, participated in the 10 August insurrection, and exemplified the transition from civic mobilization to mass revolutionary warfare.
subjects.stance: Their presence bypassed the royal veto of a formal camp and gave provincial patriotic force a decisive role in Parisian politics.

evidence.evidence_summary: Servan's proposed camp of twenty thousand provincial National Guards establishes the political issue.
The Country in Danger decree and Bastille anniversary bring fédérés into Paris despite the veto.
Invasion and the Brunswick threat deepen the emergency's democratizing consequences.
Fédérés form a key element of the forces attacking the Tuileries on 10 August.
Large-scale volunteering after the massacres points toward a transformed style of warfare.

relationships.rationale: Provincial volunteers join the armed insurrection.

subjects.label: Brunswick Manifesto
subjects.meaning: The allied commander's 25 July declaration threatened Paris with exemplary vengeance if the royal family were harmed and stated coalition aims of restoring royal and religious authority.
subjects.stance: Designed to intimidate, the declaration instead accelerated arming, democratization of the National Guard, and demands for deposition.

evidence.evidence_summary: Details the declaration's threats and its immediate radicalizing consequences in Paris.

relationships.rationale: The invasion threat intensifies deposition demands.

subjects.label: Paris Commune of 1792
subjects.meaning: The sectional committee seized municipal power as an insurrectionary Commune on 10 August, displaced the Assembly as the effective authority, directed repression, resisted new elections, and helped coordinate the September killings.
subjects.stance: The Commune is treated as savior by its supporters and as a coercive rival authority whose vengeance shaped the post-monarchical regime.

evidence.evidence_summary: The sectional committee proclaims an insurrectionary Commune and commands the forces sent against the Tuileries.
The Commune dominates the Assembly and demands vengeance against royalists, priests, and Lafayette.
It rejects disbandment, controls prison surveillance, and coordinates rather than stops the massacres.
The Commune pays participants in the prison killings and becomes an object of enduring political blame.

relationships.rationale: The insurrectionary Commune directs the assault; it formed before the palace fell.
The Commune subordinates the rump Assembly.
Commune coordination and encouragement are narrower than a claim of sole origination.

subjects.label: Danton in the August–September crisis
subjects.meaning: Danton connected sectional organization, ministerial power, mass mobilization, and emergency rhetoric while sometimes restraining the Commune's most dangerous arrests.
subjects.stance: He is shown as a powerful radical organizer and minister, but not reduced to responsibility for the September Massacres.

evidence.evidence_summary: Danton leads the Théâtre-Français section in opening its assembly beyond active citizens.
He becomes justice minister to retain sansculotte support and dominates emergency measures after invasion news.
He blocks proposed arrests by the Commune and responds to invasion with mass volunteering and defiant rhetoric.
His election to the Convention ends his service as minister.

subjects.priority_status: provisional_local_requirement; whole-book calibration reserved for synthesis

subjects.label: Counterrevolutionary suspicion, repression and surveillance in 1792
subjects.meaning: War and internal-enemy fears expanded surveillance and repression, culminating after 10 August in political justice, clerical deportation, passports and certificates of civism, searches and mass arrests. Longwy and Verdun made imprisoned suspects appear dangerous, without establishing the alleged conspiracies.
subjects.stance: Genuine military danger and politically powerful suspicions must be distinguished from proof of betrayal; the post-August measures provide the principal institutional treatment.
acceptable_access: Counterrevolutionary suspicion, repression and surveillance in 1792

evidence.evidence_summary: Local political experience teaches new deputies to identify refractory clergy as domestic enemies.
Royal veto is interpreted through a broad alleged palace-emigre-foreign conspiracy.
Southern rumor turns an accidental-looking disaster into evidence of a coordinated counter-revolutionary plot.
Military defeat prompts surveillance, disbandment, deportation, and claims that betrayal is everywhere.
A special tribunal, deportation law, arrests, passports, civic certificates, and mass searches expand coercive control.
Overcrowded prisons and fear of a counter-revolutionary breakout become immediate preconditions of the September Massacres.
Most massacre victims prove not to be politically dangerous despite perpetrators' belief in a prison conspiracy.

relationships.rationale: Searches and overcrowding combine with invasion and prison-plot panic.

subjects.label: Girondins and Montagnards, emerging factional conflict
subjects.meaning: Disputes over the Commune, responsibility for the massacres, the king's status, and an appeal to the people hardened Brissot's circle and the Mountain into rival political groupings.
subjects.stance: The source presents the split as emerging through the crises of late 1792 rather than as a fully formed division at the Convention's opening.
acceptable_access: Girondins and Montagnards, emerging factional conflict

evidence.evidence_summary: Robespierre labels Brissot's circle the Girondin faction amid conflict over the Paris Commune.
Brissot and Robespierre's camps trade accusations of complicity in the September Massacres.
The Parisian high-bench deputies cohere as the Mountain around demands to try and punish the king.
The Girondin appeal to the people makes the king's punishment a major line of factional division.
The close votes on death and reprieve expose the scale and consequences of division within the Convention.

subjects.label: Marseilles, Arles, and regional radicalism
subjects.meaning: Marseilles asserted regional primacy through armed intervention at Aix, Arles, and Avignon, helping polarize the south and destroy the Chiffon counter-revolutionary center.
subjects.stance: Local rivalry and revolutionary alignment reinforced one another; Parisian absorption in war enabled the intervention.

evidence.evidence_summary: Marseillais forces intervene at Avignon, Aix, and Arles and expel the Chiffon leaders.
The regional confrontation forms the background to wider rural anti-feudal violence.
Its delayed contingent enters Paris singing the Rhine Army hymn and becomes central to federe politics.

subjects.label: Pétion, mayoralty and radical politics
subjects.meaning: Pétion's election as Paris mayor, conduct during 20 June, suspension and restoration, role in the deposition demand, and later divergence from Robespierre place him at several turning points.
subjects.stance: His position shifted within the radical camp and cannot be reduced to a consistent Robespierrist alignment.

evidence.evidence_summary: Pétion defeats Lafayette decisively to become mayor of Paris.
He disperses the 20 June demonstrators, is suspended for failing to prevent the event, and becomes a popular rallying cause.
His restoration becomes a demand of federes and a concession around the 14 July festival.
He presents the demand for the king's deposition in the name of the Paris sections.
Now drifting from Robespierre, he moves that the Convention formally try the king.

subjects.label: Marat and advocacy of revolutionary massacre
subjects.meaning: Marat moved from marginal extremism to communal influence after 10 August, openly urged massacre, joined the surveillance committee, and won election to the Convention.
subjects.stance: He helped normalize the language of massacre, though the source does not make him the sole organizer of the September killings.
acceptable_access: Marat and advocacy of revolutionary massacre

evidence.evidence_summary: After 10 August Marat gains influence by advocating massacre of prisoners and political enemies.
The Commune places him on its prison surveillance committee shortly before the massacres.
Journalistic notoriety helps secure his election to the Convention.

relationships.rationale: Marat promotes massacre without being its sole cause.

subjects.label: Dumouriez, war ministry and Valmy
subjects.meaning: Dumouriez became foreign minister as an anti-Austrian soldier, pursued last-minute diplomacy, left the ministry for field command, and joined Kellermann in stopping the Prussians at Valmy.
subjects.stance: He combined pro-war policy with pragmatic negotiation and effective military leadership.

evidence.evidence_summary: He enters the pro-war ministry while still trying to negotiate Prussian neutrality.
He leaves the ministry for command on the northern front during the June crisis.
Dumouriez and Kellermann command the French forces that halt the Prussians at Valmy.
He opens negotiations after Valmy, nearly ending the war at that point.

subjects.label: La Marseillaise and revolutionary war culture
subjects.meaning: Rouget de Lisle composed the Army of the Rhine's battle hymn in April; Marseilles volunteers carried it into Paris, where it acquired its enduring name and political association.
subjects.stance: The anthem expressed the war's early defiance and bloodthirsty popular nationalism.
acceptable_access: La Marseillaise and revolutionary war culture

evidence.evidence_summary: Rouget de Lisle composes the battle hymn for the Army of the Rhine at Strasbourg.
Marseilles fédérés sing the hymn on entering Paris, giving it the name La Marseillaise.

subjects.label: Guillotine, introduction and political use
subjects.meaning: Retention of capital punishment led to adoption of a supposedly reliable, egalitarian, and painless mechanical decapitator, first used on a highwayman and then for political execution after 10 August.
subjects.stance: Its introduction joined humanitarian and egalitarian claims to a rapidly expanding politics of punitive violence.

evidence.evidence_summary: Explains the machine's legislative background, claimed qualities, naming, and first execution on 25 April.
The 17 August tribunal sends its first political victim to the guillotine on 21 August.
Commune activists' anger at the tribunal's pace feeds support for prison massacre and improvised courts.

subjects.label: Avignon prison massacre, October 1791
subjects.meaning: Annexationists retaliated for the lynching of a municipal official by killing papal supporters imprisoned in the former papal palace.
subjects.stance: The massacre is a significant regional example feeding national debate over refractory clergy and later southern retaliation narratives.

evidence.evidence_summary: Reports the retaliatory killing of roughly sixty papal supporters during the Assembly's clerical debate.
The massacre becomes one element in the rumor-driven cycle of regional vengeance.

reader_tasks.question: Trace how constitutional monarchy moved from the October 1791 accommodation to suspension on 10 August 1792.
Explain why Brissotins, the royal family, generals, and other deputies supported war for incompatible reasons.
Compare Brissot's regenerative case for war with Robespierre's warnings about dictatorship, defeat, and domestic enemies.
Follow the refractory-priest problem from the Assembly's opening priorities through veto conflict and post-10 August deportation.
Explain how the Saint-Domingue uprising connected colonial policy, slavery, Bordeaux interests, sugar scarcity, and Parisian price-fixing.
Connect currency decline, provisioning, and grain or sugar unrest to revived popular organization.
Explain the causes and meaning assigned to southern anti-feudal violence in spring 1792.
Trace the organizational path from popular societies and 20 June through federes, democratized sections, and the 10 August insurrection.
Explain how the Brunswick Manifesto and military reverses accelerated democratization and deposition demands.
Identify how power shifted from the Legislative Assembly to the insurrectionary Commune after 10 August.
Reconstruct the causes, actors, victims, scale, and political afterlife of the September Massacres without treating most victims as genuine counter-revolutionaries.
Explain the relationship between invasion panic, internal repression, volunteering, and Valmy.
Describe how the Convention was elected, who served in it, and why political continuity remained high despite broad male suffrage.
Trace the emerging Girondin-Montagnard division from conflict over the Commune through the appeal-to-the-people debate.
Reconstruct the legal arguments, four roll calls, execution, and consequences of the trial of Louis XVI.
